## The problem

Introductory STEM courses act as gates. A course that grades a group of students well below their own average
elsewhere can push them out of a major without anyone noticing.

## Data

Student-record and student-course tables: one row per student, one row per student-course. The public repos
carry a synthetic version (about 139,000 students and 1.3 million course records) built for the Practical
Learning Analytics course.

## Approach

Grade in a course compared with grade point average in other courses (GPAO); propensity-score matching with
`optmatch`; course-to-course persistence; treemaps and bar charts of course pathways before, during and after
a course; student networks rendered with Gephi.

## Results

- At Michigan, large STEM lecture courses graded students about 0.22 letter grades below their record elsewhere,
  and graded women about 0.1 lower than comparable men; labs showed a small bonus and no gender gap. In physics
  the gap came from timed exams, not homework ([arXiv 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.07565))
- Across five Big Ten universities and 1.1 million enrollments, 74% of STEM lecture courses gave grade penalties
  while 64% of labs gave bonuses, and the lecture gender gap held across campuses, disciplines and terms
  ([AERA Open 2017](https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858417743754))
- The same grade-anomaly measure later anchored a six-university study linking systemic advantage to grade
  penalties ([IJ STEM Ed 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-024-00474-7))
